title: Noether's symmetry
eyebrow: CETI · every symmetry hides something that stays
lede: 3,000 orbit states sit in a measured glass cube as a tangle; the cube's axes re-label and the same dots slide onto shells; one real orbit, Earth, shows distance times speed equal at both ends; a tiny network repeats the move in a second glass box.
captions: Everything moves. A few things never change.
A rule handed down? Or something that follows?
In 1918, Emmy Noether found where such rules come from.
Each dot is one moment of one orbit.
3,000 dots: ten moments of each of 300 orbits.
Simulated orbits: tangled, no pattern.
Now one real orbit: Earth around the Sun.
Closest to the Sun: 147.095 million km.
Speed there: 30.29 km/s.
Farthest: 152.100 million km.
Speed there: 29.29 km/s.
Multiply distance by speed.
Closest: 4,455.5.
Farthest: 4,455.0.
Only 0.011 % apart.
Why does it stay? Back to the 3,000 dots.
New axes: each orbit's spin, not its place.
Same 3,000 dots.
300 orbits, 300 specks.
The specks sit on 6 shells.
Inside one orbit: under 1 in a trillion of change.
A slice through the shells. Each cut shows rings.
62 orbits lit: ten dots on each of them.
New axes again: energy up, size of spin outward.
Energy sorts them into 5 layers.
Turning gives shells. Waiting gives layers.
Now no planets: a tiny network learning.
Each dot is one step of training.
3,000 steps from 100 runs.
Known since 2018: some sums stay fixed.
New axes: the sum that should not change.
The same picture: 3 shells.
The weights travel 0.24.
The fixed sum moves 0.00095.
About 250 times less.
Smoke rings too: swap the air, the swirl stays.
Monday: ask it of your own data.

brand.takeaway: Every symmetry hides something that stays.
